The Karut croaker (Johnius carutta) attains an ultimate total length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger sciaenids inhabiting the coastal waters of the Indo-Pacific region. Field surveys conducted in the estuaries of eastern India indicate that individuals approach this maximum dimension only after several years of growth, with the length-weight relationship conforming closely to the equation typical for the family. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, calculated from this morphometric relationship, reaches 686.4 grams [Wwi = 686.4 grams], a body mass that reflects the robust, deep-bodied profile characteristic of this demersal predator. Juveniles and young adults exhibit a notably rapid increase in mass during their first two years, after which the growth rate decelerates markedly as the fish approach their asymptotic dimensions. This pattern of decelerating growth is common among tropical sciaenids and is thought to be linked to the energetic demands of reproductive maturation and the seasonal availability of prey resources such as penaeid shrimps and small teleosts.

Sexual maturation in Johnius carutta begins when individuals reach a total length of 11.5 centimeters [Lp = 11.5 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 15 g [Wwp = 15 g]rams. This relatively modest size at maturity, compared to the species' ultimate dimensions, suggests an early onset of reproductive activity that may confer a demographic advantage in environments with high natural mortality rates. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected in the Hooghly-Matlah estuarine system reveals that vitellogenesis commences during the pre-monsoon months, with the first spawning event occurring shortly thereafter. The size at which 50 percent of individuals are reproductively active has been estimated from length-frequency distributions, and this value aligns well with direct observations of gonad development. Such an early maturation strategy is consistent with the life-history pattern observed in many small-to-medium-sized croakers that inhabit turbid, productive estuaries where predation pressure on juveniles is intense.

Reproductive output in the Karut croaker has been quantified through controlled laboratory observations conducted at a stable water temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, females produce approximately 15 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 15 eggs per spawning event] across multiple clutches throughout an extended breeding season lasting several months. Field estimates of spawning frequency indicate that an individual female can release roughly 4 clutches annually [F_R_i = roughly 4 clutches annually], a rate that appears to be sustained by the high productivity of the estuarine environment during the monsoon and post-monsoon periods. The daily reproduction rate reconstructed from these sub-components is substantial for a fish of this size and reflects a life-history strategy oriented toward high fecundity rather than prolonged parental investment. Egg diameter averages one millimeter, and hatching success in captivity exceeds seventy percent when water quality remains optimal.

The wet weight at birth, corresponding to the newly hatched yolk-sac larva, is approximately 0.00053 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00053 grams], reflecting the small egg size and lecithotrophic larval phase typical of Johnius carutta. After chorion rupture, the prolarva measures roughly two millimeters in total length and relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves for the first three to four days of development. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs upon mouth opening and the resorption of the yolk sac, a critical period during which mortality can be high if suitable zooplanktonic prey is not available. This tiny initial mass, an order of magnitude lower than that observed in some congeneric species, suggests a trade-off between maximizing fecundity and provisioning individual offspring with energy reserves. Comparative data from related sciaenids indicate that larval survival rates are strongly dependent on water temperature and prey density during this early stage.

Longevity in Johnius carutta, deduced from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age estimation, reaches a maximum of approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] under natural conditions, with individuals maintained at a water temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C] exhibiting somewhat slower senescence than those exposed to wider thermal fluctuations. This lifespan is relatively short compared to that of many temperate sciaenids, a pattern often attributed to the accelerated metabolic rates and higher natural mortality characteristic of tropical fish populations. The oldest individuals captured in estuarine surveys typically display worn dentition and reduced gonadal output, suggesting that reproductive senescence precedes somatic death by a measurable interval. Population matrix models incorporating this maximum longevity, together with the age at first reproduction and fecundity estimates, indicate that the intrinsic rate of increase is sufficient to sustain the species under moderate fishing pressure. Nevertheless, the combination of early maturation and a compressed adult lifespan renders this croaker particularly sensitive to overexploitation of spawning aggregations.
